theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The Permanent Secretary of a ministry asks her directors to manage innovation and continuous improvement together. What is the main difference between the two?
options: Innovation brings in new ideas; improvement refines current ways
Innovation is for private firms; improvement is for public bodies
Innovation needs no evidence; improvement needs a full audit first
Innovation is done by IT staff; improvement is done by managers

questions.stem: A government sets up one shared service unit to handle human resource work for five ministries, changing how that work is organised. Which type of innovation is this?
options: Product innovation in a new item for public sale
Incremental innovation to a single existing form
Organisational innovation in how work is set up
Technological innovation in new office equipment

questions.stem: A parish municipal corporation adds a text-message reminder to its existing property tax notices. Which type of innovation is this?
options: Radical innovation that replaces the service
Incremental innovation to an existing process
Disruptive innovation that creates a new market
Organisational innovation in reporting lines

questions.stem: A director at a government agency wants to set up an innovation programme for the whole agency. What should she link it to first?
options: The newest technology on the market this year
The ideas put forward by the most senior manager
Whatever budget is left at the end of the year
The agency's strategic goals and corporate plan

questions.stem: An agency redesigning its complaints service invites a group of customers, including elderly people from rural St Elizabeth, to help design it. What is this approach called?

options: Closed innovation within the agency's units

questions.stem: An agency's innovation committee receives 60 ideas but can fund only five this year. What is the best way to choose?
options: Score each against agreed criteria such as impact and cost
Fund the ideas put forward by the most senior officers
Fund the first five ideas that reached the committee
Pick the ideas that would cause the least disruption

questions.stem: An innovation committee scores three ideas out of 10, with weights of 50% for impact, 30% for cost and 20% for ease. Idea A scores 8, 6 and 5; Idea B scores 6, 9 and 8; Idea C scores 9, 4 and 6. Which idea has the highest weighted score?
options: Idea A
Idea B
Idea C

questions.stem: In a stage-gate process for innovations, what happens at each "gate"?
options: Staff vote on who will lead the next stage
The project budget is doubled automatically
The idea is published for public comment

questions.stem: Before asking for funds to roll out a new online licensing service, what should a director prepare?

A press release announcing the start of the service

options: To delay spending until the next financial year
To give the two offices an advantage over others

A new online renewal system costs J$6,000,000 to set up and saves J$1,500,000 a year in staff time and printing. What is the simple payback period?
options: 2.5 years
9 years
0.25 years
4 years

questions.stem: When a new case-management system is rolled out across an agency, a few keen officers use it at once and help their colleagues. In the diffusion of innovations model, who are they?
options: Early adopters

options: Ask the other body to slow down its own process

questions.stem: Which measure best shows whether an agency's innovation programme is producing results?
options: The number of meetings held by the committee
The number of posters put up about innovation
The share of ideas put into use and their benefits

questions.stem: Last year staff sent 240 ideas to a ministry's idea system and 36 were put into practice. What was the implementation rate?
Why should an agency judge its innovation work on service quality, staff engagement and learning as well as cost savings?
options: Cost misses gains for citizens, staff and learning
Cost savings in public bodies can never be measured
Several indicators make poor results easier to hide
A single indicator would need approval from outside

questions.stem: A director wants to test a new idea quickly, but it means spending public money with a supplier the agency has not used before. What must she do?
options: Pay the supplier in cash to save time

questions.stem: A board says it has a low risk appetite for public safety but a higher risk appetite for new ways of serving customers online. What does this tell managers?
options: No new ideas may be tried in any area of work

That the staff in both agencies agree to the sharing

questions.stem: Officers from several ministries who lead improvement projects meet online each month to share methods and problems. What is this kind of group called?
options: A steering committee
A community of practice
A tender evaluation panel

questions.stem: Which way of recognising staff who make improvements is most likely to keep ideas coming across an agency?
options: Naming only those whose ideas save the most money
Thanking people promptly and showing what changed

Giving rewards only to managers who lead projects

questions.stem: Ideas at an agency stall because every change needs sign-off from five separate committees. Which barrier is this?
options: Low staff skill
Weak customer demand
Lack of technology

questions.stem: Two units in a ministry are each improving the same grant application process without knowing about the other. What should the director do?
options: Bring them together under one coordinated project
Let both carry on and pick the faster one later
Stop both projects and keep the old process
Ask each unit to keep its work confidential

questions.stem: A ministry wants to support innovation in its agencies, but each agency says it has no spare budget. Which option would help most?
options: Ask staff to fund ideas from their own pay
Remove all innovation from the corporate plan
Set up a small innovation fund with clear rules

questions.stem: A year after rolling out a new online service, what should the agency review first?
options: Whether the expected benefits were achieved
Whether the logo on the website still looks fresh
How many staff liked the project manager

questions.stem: A trial of self-service kiosks at a tax office is stopped after three months because few people use them. How should leaders treat this?
options: As proof that innovation never works in public bodies
As a reason to discipline the project team
As learning to record, and a sign to adjust or stop
As something to leave out of the annual report

questions.stem: Before an agency moves a service online only, why should it consider citizens who have no internet access?
options: They are a small group who can be left out
They can always go to a private internet café
Digital public services are not allowed by law
Public services must stay open and fair to all

questions.stem: A planned improvement would change officers' working hours at a public body. Who should be consulted early?
options: Only the press office, once the change is final
The staff affected and their union or association
The supplier of the new rostering software system
No one, as working hours are for managers to decide

questions.stem: An agency made an improvement two years ago, and its results have now levelled off. What does continuous improvement suggest?
options: The improvement work is finished for good
The process should go back to the old method
Results that level off need no more measuring
Review it again and look for the next gain

questions.stem: An innovation committee funds only safe, small projects year after year. Why might this be a weakness?
options: It leaves out bolder ideas that could bring large gains
Small projects are not allowed in public bodies at all
Safe projects always cost more than bold ones
Small projects can never be measured or reported

questions.stem: During work time and with agency equipment, an officer develops a new tool for scheduling inspections. Who would usually own the tool?
options: The officer alone
The agency
The software supplier

questions.stem: A director wants every member of staff to understand a new organisation-wide improvement programme. Which approach is best?
options: A single email sent from head office
A notice pinned to the staff canteen board
Briefings, early success stories and open forums
A policy saved to the shared drive without notice

options: Asking her to come back if problems appear
Writing the new method into procedures and training

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one word describes an innovation that changes a service so much that it replaces the old way of working entirely?
In the diffusion of innovations model, what name is given to the last group of people to take up a new idea?
What five-letter abbreviation names the Six Sigma improvement cycle of define, measure, analyse, improve and control?
What term names the documented set of policies, processes and responsibilities an organisation uses to manage the quality of its services?
What one word names a small-scale trial of a new idea in one place before it is rolled out across the organisation?
What term names the practice of comparing an organisation's processes and results with those of the best similar organisations, in order to learn from them?
A new system costs J$5,400,000 and saves J$450,000 a month. What is its payback period, in months?
What word names an early, simple model of a new service or tool, built quickly so that users can try it and give feedback?
What two-word term describes an approach to innovation that draws on ideas from outside the organisation, such as universities, firms and citizens?
What term names a process in which an innovation passes through set stages, with a go or stop decision between each stage?
Errors on 10,000 forms a year fell from 5% to 2% of forms. How many fewer forms a year had errors?
What two-word term describes the amount and type of risk a board is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives?
What two-word term names a human-centred approach to innovation that starts by understanding users, then defines the problem, generates ideas, builds prototypes and tests them?
An agency processes 8,000 applications a month at a total cost of J$2,400,000. What is the cost per application, in J$?
What term names the stage at which a proven innovation is extended from a pilot site to the whole organisation?

essays.stem: Compare innovation with continuous improvement, and explain why a public body needs both. Use examples from a ministry, agency or parish municipal corporation.
essays.modelAnswer: Continuous improvement is the steady, step-by-step refining of the way existing work is done: cutting delays, errors and waste in a process the organisation already runs. For example, a parish municipal corporation might redesign its building-plan checklist so that fewer applications are sent back. Innovation is the introduction of something new to the organisation: a new service, a new way of delivering it or a new way of organising work. For example, a tax agency might launch a mobile app for filing and paying. Improvement is usually low in risk and cost and draws on the people who do the work, while innovation carries more uncertainty, often needs investment and a business case, and must be tested in pilots. A public body needs both. Without improvement, everyday services stay slow and costly and staff lose confidence. Without innovation, the body cannot meet new needs, use new technology or make large gains in value for money. Leaders should run both through one framework, linked to the corporate plan, with shared measures and learning.
markingPoints: Clear definition of continuous improvement with an example
Clear definition of innovation with an example
Compares risk, cost, scale or who is involved
Explains why a public body needs both
Links both to strategy or a single framework

essays.stem: Staff at a statutory body fear blame and rarely suggest new ideas. Plan how you, as a senior manager, would build a culture of innovation across the organisation.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out why people are afraid, through a short anonymous survey and small group discussions, so that the plan answers real concerns. Leaders must then set the example: the chief executive and directors should say clearly that well-planned trials may fail, admit their own mistakes and ask for challenge in meetings. I would set up a simple, open way to put forward ideas, such as an online system with a promise of a reply within two weeks, and make sure every idea gets a fair hearing against published criteria. Small budgets and time for staff to test ideas would show that the organisation is serious. When a trial fails, we would hold a no-blame review and share what was learned. Successes would be recognised quickly and publicly, giving credit to the people who did the work. Innovation would be added to managers' objectives and to induction. I would track the number of ideas, how many are used, and repeat the staff survey after a year to check whether attitudes have changed.
markingPoints: Finds the causes of fear before acting
Leaders model the behaviour and accept intelligent failure
Sets up an open, fair system for ideas with feedback
Provides resources and recognition
Builds it into objectives and measures the change in culture

essays.stem: An agency's innovation committee can fund one idea this year. Idea X, an online booking system, costs J$8,000,000 and is expected to save J$2,000,000 a year. Idea Y, a mobile service unit, costs J$4,500,000 and is expected to save J$900,000 a year, and it would also reach rural customers who cannot travel to an office. Work out the payback period of each idea and recommend, with reasons, which to fund first.
essays.modelAnswer: The payback period is the cost divided by the yearly saving. For Idea X it is J$8,000,000 divided by J$2,000,000, which is 4 years. For Idea Y it is J$4,500,000 divided by J$900,000, which is 5 years. On payback alone, Idea X is better, because it recovers its cost a year sooner and saves more each year. However, a public body must also think about its purpose and fairness, not only money. Idea Y costs J$3,500,000 less, so it is easier to fund, and it would reach rural and elderly customers who are now poorly served, which may support the agency's goals on access. Idea X may also leave out people without internet access. I would recommend funding Idea X first if the agency's main goal this year is efficiency, but only with an assisted option at offices for people who cannot go online. I would also ask the committee to score both ideas against the agency's strategic criteria, check the savings estimates and risks, and plan to fund Idea Y next year.
markingPoints: Idea X payback correctly worked out as 4 years
Idea Y payback correctly worked out as 5 years
Considers non-financial benefits such as access and fairness
Notes limits of payback or checks estimates and risks
Gives a clear recommendation with reasons

essays.stem: Describe how you would design a system, for a whole government agency, for collecting, screening and acting on ideas from staff and the public.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a short policy that explains the purpose of the system, who may take part and how ideas will be handled, approved by the senior team. Ideas would come in through one simple channel, such as an online form that staff and the public can reach by phone or computer, with paper forms in offices for those who need them. Each idea would be logged and acknowledged within a few days. A small panel with members from different units would screen ideas monthly against published criteria, such as fit with the corporate plan, benefit to customers, cost, risk and ease of use. Simple ideas could be passed straight to the unit concerned to try. Larger ideas would move through stages: a short business case, a pilot with clear measures, and then a decision to scale, change or stop. Every person would be told what happened to their idea and why. The system would have a small budget, a named owner and a dashboard showing ideas received, used and their benefits, reviewed by the senior team each quarter.
markingPoints: Policy, purpose and ownership of the system
Easy, accessible channels with logging and acknowledgement
Fair screening against stated criteria
Staged path: business case, pilot, scale or stop
Feedback to contributors and monitoring of results

essays.stem: A ministry has piloted an online appointment system in two parish offices for six months. Explain how you would evaluate the pilot and decide whether to roll it out across the island.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the success measures agreed before the pilot, such as waiting time, missed appointments, customer satisfaction, staff time and cost per visit, and compare the pilot offices with their own baseline and with two similar offices that did not take part. I would gather the system data, run a short customer survey, including people who chose not to book online, and hold group discussions with staff. I would look for problems such as customers without internet access, technical faults or extra work for staff, and check whether the system meets the data protection law. I would then work out the full cost of a national roll-out, including training, equipment and support, and compare it with the expected benefits. If the results are good and hold in both offices, I would recommend a phased roll-out with the faults fixed and a walk-in option kept. If the results are mixed, I would extend or change the pilot. The report to the Permanent Secretary would set out the evidence, the lessons learned and the recommendation.
markingPoints: Uses agreed measures and compares with a baseline or control
Gathers views of customers and staff
Checks problems, access, risks and legal points
Weighs full roll-out costs against benefits
Makes a justified decision: roll out in phases, change or stop

essays.stem: Compare Lean and Six Sigma as approaches to organisation-wide improvement in a public body, and recommend where each would fit best.
essays.modelAnswer: Lean focuses on flow and waste. It maps a process from start to end, separates the steps that add value for the customer from those that do not, such as waiting, rework, extra handling and unnecessary approvals, and removes the waste so that the work flows faster. It is quick to learn and suits processes with long delays. Six Sigma focuses on variation and errors. It uses the DMAIC cycle (define, measure, analyse, improve, control) and data to find the root causes of defects and to make results consistent. It needs more skill in data and statistics and usually trained project leaders. In a public body, Lean would fit best where customers complain of delays, such as a passport or licensing office where files sit in trays between short steps. Six Sigma would fit best where accuracy is critical, such as pension or benefit calculations where errors cost money and public trust. Many bodies combine them. I would recommend starting with Lean for quick, visible gains, and using Six Sigma for a few complex, high-risk processes.
markingPoints: Explains Lean: flow, value and waste
Explains Six Sigma: variation, errors and DMAIC with data
Compares skills, speed or type of problem
Gives a suitable public-sector example for each
Makes a reasoned recommendation

essays.stem: Explain the main barriers to innovation in public bodies, and recommend practical ways a senior manager can overcome them.
essays.modelAnswer: A first barrier is fear of blame: public servants are held to account for mistakes with public money, so they avoid anything untested. Leaders can reduce this by setting a clear risk appetite, approving small, controlled pilots and treating failed trials as learning. A second barrier is rigid rules and slow approval. Managers should keep the controls that protect public money, such as the procurement rules, but remove extra layers of sign-off and give units authority to test small ideas. A third barrier is the yearly budget cycle, which leaves no money for new ideas; a small innovation fund with simple rules helps. A fourth is working in silos, where units do not share ideas; cross-unit teams and communities of practice break this down. A fifth is lack of skills and time, which training in improvement methods and protected time can address. Finally, change fatigue and resistance can be eased by involving staff and citizens early, explaining the reasons and showing early results. The senior team should review these barriers each year through staff surveys.
markingPoints: Identifies fear of blame or risk aversion with a remedy
Identifies rules, approvals or budget limits with a remedy
Identifies silos, skills or resistance with a remedy
Remedies keep accountability and the law in place
Practical and suited to a public body

essays.stem: Explain how a public body can manage the risks of innovation while still being accountable for public money and following the law.
essays.modelAnswer: A public body must balance the need to try new things with its duty to use public money properly and treat citizens fairly. First, the board should set a risk appetite that shows where bold ideas are welcome, for example online services, and where caution is needed, such as public safety. Each larger innovation should have a business case and a risk assessment, with risks entered in a risk register, an owner for each risk and actions to reduce them. Testing through small pilots limits the money and the number of people affected if something goes wrong. Spending must follow the procurement rules for public bodies, and contracts must protect the body's interests, including ownership of anything developed. Any use of personal data must meet the data protection law, and services must stay open to people without internet access. Decisions and their reasons should be recorded so that auditors and the public can see why money was spent. Regular reports to the board, and honest reporting of both results and failures, keep the body accountable.
markingPoints: Sets a risk appetite or tolerance
Business case, risk assessment and risk register with owners
Uses pilots to limit exposure
Follows procurement and data protection rules and keeps services fair
Records decisions and reports openly for accountability

essays.stem: Describe the indicators you would use to judge how well a government agency's innovation and continuous improvement programme is working, and justify your choice.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use a small, balanced set of indicators so that the senior team sees the whole picture. Activity indicators would include the number of ideas received and the share of staff who have taken part; these show whether people are engaged, but on their own they say nothing about results. Process indicators would include the average time from idea to decision and the share of ideas put into practice; these show whether the system is working smoothly. Outcome indicators matter most: changes in customer waiting time, error rates, customer satisfaction and cost per transaction for the services that were improved, measured against a baseline. Financial indicators would include savings and the payback on innovation spending, to show value for public money. People indicators would include staff engagement scores and how many staff are trained in improvement methods, because these build the capacity for future change. Learning would be shown by the number of lessons-learned reviews completed and shared. Each indicator would have a target, an owner and a data source, and would be reported quarterly on a dashboard.
markingPoints: Includes activity or participation measures
Includes outcome measures for customers and services against a baseline
Includes financial or value-for-money measures
Includes people, capacity or learning measures
Justifies the balance, with targets, owners and reporting

essays.stem: Explain how a large public body can capture and share what it learns from innovation projects, including those that fail, so that the whole organisation benefits.
essays.modelAnswer: Learning is lost when it stays in the heads of a project team or in a report that nobody reads. At the end of each project, and at key stages, the team should hold a short no-blame review asking what was planned, what happened, why, and what should be done differently. The findings should be written in a standard, brief lessons-learned format and stored in one searchable place, such as an intranet library, tagged by topic so that others can find them. Failed projects are just as valuable, because they stop other units repeating costly mistakes, so leaders must make it safe to report them honestly. Knowledge should also be shared through people: communities of practice, lunchtime talks, short videos, and moving experienced staff onto new projects. New projects should be required to check the library at the start. Senior managers can show that learning matters by asking about lessons in reviews and by telling stories of failures that led to success. The quality unit should check each year that lessons are being used.
markingPoints: Holds structured no-blame reviews during and after projects
Records lessons in a standard, searchable store
Values and shares lessons from failures
Shares through people and networks such as communities of practice
Makes new projects use the lessons and checks this

practical1.title: Design an innovation and improvement framework for a public agency
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up government agency (for example a parish municipal corporation, a ministry's licensing agency or a public hospital), with its corporate plan goals, a staff survey summary and a list of eight ideas sent in by staff and customers. As a group, design a framework for managing innovation and continuous improvement across the whole agency, and produce: a one-page policy statement (purpose, who can take part, how ideas are handled, risk appetite); a poster or slide showing the idea pipeline with its stages and decision gates; a scoring matrix in a spreadsheet that applies weighted criteria to all eight ideas and ranks them; a governance chart showing who decides at each gate; and a dashboard of six indicators with targets and owners. Give each member a named role: chair (keeps time and writes the policy statement), pipeline designer, analyst (builds and checks the scoring matrix), governance lead, and measures lead (dashboard). In a group of four, the chair also does the governance chart. Each member explains their part to the assessor. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: agency profile, corporate plan goals, staff survey summary and eight ideas
Computers with word-processing, spreadsheet and presentation software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
Printer or a way to show the work on screen
photos: The group's planning notes with roles shared out
The idea pipeline poster or slide with its gates
The scoring matrix on screen with the eight ideas ranked
The indicator dashboard with targets and owners
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The framework links clearly to the agency's corporate plan goals
The pipeline has clear stages, gates and stop or go decisions
The scoring criteria and weights are sensible and the sums are correct
Governance shows who decides and keeps public accountability
Indicators are balanced, measurable and have targets and owners
Explained their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names; no real staff or citizens
Keep the case pack and the group's scores confidential to the group and assessor
Treat each member's ideas with respect and let everyone speak
Share the workload fairly and take short breaks from the screen

practical2.title: Present a business case and pilot plan to an innovation committee (role play)
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a public service problem (for example long queues at a tax office in Spanish Town, missed clinic appointments in a rural parish, or slow processing of trade licences). As a group, develop one innovation to solve it and present it to an innovation committee, played by the assessor and members of another group. First, interview two "service users" (played by members of another group) for ten minutes and note what they need. Then produce: a one-page business case with options, costs, savings and the payback period, worked out and checked twice; a pilot plan with the site, length, success measures, baseline and timeline as a Gantt chart; a risk table covering public money, procurement, data protection and access for people without internet; and five slides. Give each member a named role: user researcher (runs the interviews and summarises needs), finance analyst (costs and payback), pilot planner (plan and Gantt chart), risk and compliance officer (risk table), and lead presenter (slides and timing). In a group of four, the lead presenter also does the user research summary. Every member presents their part and answers at least one question from the committee.
materials: Problem card and cost data from the assessor
Computers with word-processing, spreadsheet and presentation software
A screen or projector for the presentation
photos: The interview notes from the two service users
The business case with the payback sum
The pilot plan and Gantt chart
The presentation to the committee, with the slides showing
The committee's question sheet with the group's answers noted
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The innovation answers the needs found in the interviews
Costs, savings and payback are worked out correctly
The pilot has clear measures, a baseline and a realistic timeline
Risks to public money, data and fair access are identified with actions
Presented their part clearly and within time
Answered the committee's questions with reasons
